entries_new.name: Muscovy Company
aka: Company of Merchant Adventurers to New Lands
entries_new.founder: Thomas White, Richard Chancellor, Sebastian Cabot and Sir Hugh Willoughby (founders of the predecessor company, 1551)
entries_new.stopped_by: Monopoly ended in 1698
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter gave a joint-stock company the sole right to English trade with Russia.
entries_new.story: The Muscovy Company was an English trading company chartered in 1555. Wikipedia calls it the first major chartered joint-stock company, meaning a company owned by shareholders under a royal charter. It traces back to the Company of Merchant Adventurers to New Lands, founded in 1551 by Thomas White, Richard Chancellor, Sebastian Cabot and Sir Hugh Willoughby to search for a Northeast Passage to China. The charter gave it a monopoly on trade between England and Russia until 1698. It survived as a trading company until the Russian Revolution and has operated as a charity since 1917.
entries_new.anchor: Moscow, Russia (centre of the trade covered by the monopoly)

entries_new.name: Astrolabe Company
entries_new.founder: Hamburg and Bremen notables and financiers; director Adolph von Hansemann
entries_new.stopped_by: Merged into the New Guinea Company in 1896 after bad harvest years
entries_new.mechanism: A private colonial society ran plantations on land taken over from the chartered New Guinea Company.
entries_new.story: The Astrolabe Company was a German colonial society in Kaiser-Wilhelmsland, founded on 27 October 1891 with a capital of 2.4 million marks by Hamburg and Bremen notables and financiers. Its director, Adolph von Hansemann, also headed the New Guinea Company, from which it took over tobacco plantations at Stephansort and Erima. It added plantations at Jomba in 1892 and Maraga in 1893, and also shipped exotic woods and tried coconut palms, Liberian coffee and rubber. After bad years in 1895 and 1896 it merged back into the New Guinea Company in 1896.
entries_new.anchor: Astrolabe Bay area, Kaiser-Wilhelmsland (approximate)

entries_new.name: London and Bristol Company
entries_new.founder: John Guy, Bristol merchant, with a syndicate of investors
entries_new.stopped_by: The Crown began granting lands to others in 1616
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter gave a company sole rights to use the land and sea of a peninsula.
entries_new.story: The London and Bristol Company, also called the Newfoundland Company, grew out of English merchants' interest in the Newfoundland fishery. John Guy, a Bristol merchant, visited Newfoundland in 1608 to find a site for a colony. After he returned, 40 people applied to be incorporated as a company. King James granted a charter on 2 May 1610 giving it a monopoly in agriculture, mining, fishing and hunting on the Avalon Peninsula. Its exclusive rights lasted until 1616, when the Crown began to grant lands to others.
entries_new.anchor: Avalon Peninsula, Newfoundland

entries_new.name: New Netherland Company
entries_new.founder: Adriaen Block, Hendrick Christiaensen and twelve other Dutch merchants
entries_new.stopped_by: Charter not renewed in 1618; replaced by the Dutch West India Company
entries_new.recognition: States General of the Dutch Republic
entries_new.mechanism: A three-year trade monopoly from the States General over a stretch of the North American coast.
entries_new.story: The New Netherland Company was a chartered company of Dutch merchants. After Henry Hudson's 1609 voyage along the east coast of North America, merchants sent ships to trade furs with Native Americans. On 11 October 1614 Block, Christiaensen and twelve other merchants petitioned the States General, which granted a monopoly of trade between the 40th and 45th parallels for three years from 1 January 1615. The charter was not renewed in 1618 because the Dutch West India Company was being prepared. Its founders kept most of the trade until that company was set up in 1621.
entries_new.anchor: Hudson River region (approximate)

entries_new.name: Compagnie de Saint-Christophe
entries_new.founder: Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc; Cardinal Richelieu was the main investor
entries_new.stopped_by: Reorganised in 1635 as the Compagnie des Iles de l'Amerique
entries_new.mechanism: A French charter let a company settle and run a Caribbean island.
entries_new.story: The Compagnie de Saint-Christophe was created and chartered by French adventurers to exploit the island of Saint-Christophe, now Saint Kitts and Nevis. In 1625 Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc landed there with a band of adventurers and some slaves. He returned to France and received a charter in 1626 from Cardinal Richelieu, who held 10,000 livres of the 45,000 livres of capital. The company was not very successful. In 1635 Richelieu had it reorganised as the Compagnie des Iles de l'Amerique to settle Saint-Christophe, Martinique and Guadeloupe.
entries_new.anchor: Saint Kitts

entries_new.name: Free Society of Traders
entries_new.founder: Nicholas More, James Claypoole and Philip Ford, with William Penn
entries_new.recognition: Concessions from William Penn, holder of a royal charter
entries_new.mechanism: A proprietor's concessions gave a company land and a share in running a young colony's economy.
entries_new.story: The Free Society of Traders was a company of merchants, landowners and associates of William Penn, mostly Quaker merchants from London and Dublin. It began as a joint-stock company launched in London in 1681 by Nicholas More, James Claypoole and Philip Ford, after Penn received his royal charter in March. Penn offered the first 100 investors 5,000 acres each plus exclusive rights to property in the capital city, and fashioned a rudimentary government from the Traders' members. Society Hill in Philadelphia is named after it.
entries_new.anchor: Philadelphia (approximate)

entries_new.name: Nanto-Bordelaise Company
aka: Compagnie de Bordeaux et de Nantes pour la Colonisation de l'Ile du Sud de la Nouvelle Zelande
entries_new.founder: Jean-Francois Langlois and merchants of Nantes and Bordeaux
entries_new.stopped_by: British acquisition of New Zealand in 1840 (Treaty of Waitangi, Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson)
entries_new.challenge: British Crown, which secured the country in 1840; the land agreement with local chiefs was disputed in scope
entries_new.cost: 1,000 francs promised for the Banks Peninsula land
entries_new.mechanism: Land bought from local chiefs and royal backing were meant to support a French claim to the South Island.
entries_new.story: The Nanto-Bordelaise Company was formed in 1839 by merchants from Nantes and Bordeaux to found a French colony in the South Island of New Zealand. Whaling captain Jean-Francois Langlois had negotiated with Ngai Tahu chiefs in 1838 to buy several thousand acres of Banks Peninsula for 1,000 francs, and the company aimed to claim the whole South Island for France. King Louis-Philippe backed it with transport for 80 settlers to Akaroa. The Treaty of Waitangi and Lieutenant-Governor Hobson's British claim came first in 1840, and the colony went ahead under a mix of French and British jurisdiction. The agreement with the chiefs proved less clear than promised.
entries_new.anchor: Akaroa, Banks Peninsula, New Zealand

entries_new.name: Guinea Company of Scotland
entries_new.founder: Monopoly granted by King Charles
entries_new.stopped_by: Loss of a ship and crew to Portuguese forces at Sao Tome; no compensation recovered
entries_new.mechanism: A royal monopoly over West African trade for a Scottish company.
entries_new.story: The Guinea Company of Scotland was a short-lived Scottish trading company of the 1630s. King Charles granted it a royal monopoly over trade with West Africa, modelled on the English Guinea Company, with which it unofficially co-operated. It made only one voyage, with two ships. One returned, and the other was seized by Portuguese forces at Sao Tome and its crew killed. The company tried to recover compensation without success and ceased to operate around 1639. Scotland made no further organised attempt to trade with Africa until the Company of Scotland in 1695.
entries_new.anchor: Sao Tome (where one ship was seized)

entries_new.name: Swedish Africa Company
entries_new.founder: Louis De Geer and Laurens De Geer
entries_new.mechanism: A Swedish trading company worked a stretch of the Gold Coast.
entries_new.story: The Swedish Africa Company was founded in 1649 on the initiative of the Walloon-Swedish merchant Louis De Geer and his son Laurens. Its main interest was trade on the Swedish Gold Coast, mainly gold and ivory, resold in Hamburg or Amsterdam. Its part in the slave trade was limited by its lack of access to American markets. During its existence it transported 300 to 400 slaves to the Portuguese sugar plantations on Sao Tome.
entries_new.anchor: Swedish Gold Coast (present-day Ghana, approximate)

entries_new.name: African Company of Merchants
aka: Company of Merchants Trading to Africa
entries_new.stopped_by: Dissolved in 1821; the Gold Coast became a British colony
entries_new.mechanism: A British chartered company administered trading posts on the Gold Coast.
entries_new.story: The African Company of Merchants, also called the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa, was a British chartered company that existed from 1752 to 1821. It administered British trading posts in the Gold Coast region of modern Ghana and engaged in the Atlantic slave trade, illegally from 1807 onwards. Controversy in Britain over its continuing involvement in the slave trade after 1807 contributed to its dissolution, and the Gold Coast became a formal British colony in 1821.
entries_new.anchor: Cape Coast, Gold Coast (approximate)

entries_new.name: Portuguese East India Company
entries_new.founder: Philip III of Portugal
entries_new.stopped_by: Failed within a short time (no cause given in the article intro)
entries_new.mechanism: A crown-chartered company meant to secure Portuguese trade and holdings in India against Dutch and English rivals.
entries_new.story: The Portuguese East India Company was a short-lived attempt by Philip III of Portugal to create a chartered company to protect Portuguese interests in India. The pressure came from the rival Dutch East India Company and English East India Company, after the personal union of the Portuguese and Spanish Crowns. Wikipedia describes it as ill-fated.
entries_new.anchor: India (approximate)

entries_new.name: Inter-Allied Rhineland High Commission
entries_new.founder: Allied powers of World War I under the Treaty of Versailles
entries_new.stopped_by: Occupation ended 30 June 1930
entries_new.mechanism: A treaty placed a region of Germany under an allied commission as security against a future German attack and as a guarantee for reparations.
entries_new.story: The Treaty of Versailles of 28 June 1919 created the Inter-Allied Rhineland High Commission to supervise the occupation of the Rhineland. It came into being on 10 January 1920, was based in Coblenz, and was led by a French commissioner with one member each from Belgium, the United Kingdom and, as an observer only, the United States. The occupation put Germany's land west of the Rhine and four bridgeheads east of it under Allied control from 1 December 1918 until 30 June 1930, and was widened to the Ruhr from 1923 to 1925. Some separatist movements tried to create an independent Rhineland allied to France, but none had significant popular support.
entries_new.anchor: Coblenz (Koblenz), Germany

entries_new.name: Chinese Eastern Railway Zone
entries_new.founder: Russian Empire, under a concession from the Qing dynasty
entries_new.stopped_by: Returned to the People's Republic of China in 1952
entries_new.challenge: Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905), the 1929 Sino-Soviet Conflict and the Second Sino-Japanese War
entries_new.recognition: Qing dynasty concession; later Soviet-Chinese treaty
entries_new.mechanism: A railway concession from the Qing government gave Russia a zone administered from Harbin.
entries_new.story: The Chinese Eastern Railway was built by the Russian Empire from 1897 to 1902 as a concession granted by the Qing dynasty government. It linked Chita with Vladivostok and with Port Arthur, and Saint Petersburg administered the railway and the concession, known as the Chinese Eastern Railway Zone, from Harbin. The southern branch became the Japanese South Manchuria Railway from 1906. The Soviet Union sold the railway to the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo in 1935, regained co-ownership by treaty in 1945, and returned it to the People's Republic of China in 1952.
entries_new.anchor: Harbin, China

entries_new.name: Saudi Arabian-Iraqi neutral zone
entries_new.founder: Uqair Protocol of 1922
entries_new.stopped_by: Partition agreement of December 1981
entries_new.recognition: Saudi Arabia and Iraq by treaty
entries_new.mechanism: Two states left a stretch of border undefined and treated it as shared ground.
entries_new.story: The Saudi Arabian-Iraqi neutral zone was a kite-shaped region of 7,044 square kilometres on the border between Saudi Arabia and Iraq where the border had not been settled. It came into existence after the Uqair Protocol of 1922, which defined the border between Mandatory Iraq and the Sultanate of Nejd. Iraqi and Saudi representatives agreed to partition it on 26 December 1981, and the Iraqi National Assembly approved on 28 January 1982. The date of the division is unknown, and notice went to the United Nations in June 1991. The population was sparse and mostly Bedouin.
entries_new.anchor: Saudi Arabia-Iraq border

entries_new.name: Peking Legation Quarter
entries_new.founder: Foreign powers with legations in Beijing
entries_new.stopped_by: Special status effectively ended by World War II
entries_new.challenge: Boxer Rebellion, which besieged the legations for 55 days in 1900
entries_new.mechanism: Foreign governments held a district of the capital under their own jurisdiction after 1900.
entries_new.story: The Peking Legation Quarter was the area of Beijing where foreign legations stood between 1861 and 1959. It was the site of the 55-day siege of the International Legations during the Boxer Rebellion in 1900. After that rebellion the quarter was under the jurisdiction of the foreign countries with legations there, and foreign residents were exempt from Chinese law. World War II effectively ended its special status.
entries_new.anchor: Dongcheng District, Beijing

entries_new.name: Allied-occupied Austria
entries_new.founder: United Kingdom, Soviet Union, United States and France
entries_new.stopped_by: Austrian State Treaty, in force 27 July 1955, after Austria promised perpetual neutrality
entries_new.recognition: Declaration of Moscow of 1943 treated Austria as the first victim of Nazi aggression
entries_new.mechanism: Four powers held zones, with a jointly run centre in the capital, until a treaty restored full independence.
entries_new.story: Austria declared independence from Nazi Germany on 27 April 1945 and was occupied by the Allies. It was divided into four occupation zones held by the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union, the United States and France. Vienna was subdivided the same way, but its central district was administered jointly by the Allied Control Council. Austria had its own government from 1945, unlike Germany. The occupation ended when the Austrian State Treaty came into force on 27 July 1955, and the last occupation troops left on 25 October 1955.
entries_new.anchor: Vienna, Austria

entries_new.name: European Commission of the Danube
entries_new.founder: Treaty of Paris (1856) signatories
entries_new.mechanism: A treaty gave an international commission authority over the river mouths.
entries_new.story: The Commissions of the Danube River were authorised by the Treaty of Paris in 1856, after the Crimean War. The European Commission of the Danube had authority over the three mouths of the river, the Chilia in the north, the Sulina in the middle and the St. George in the south. It was designed to last two years and lasted eighty-two. A separate International Danube Commission, meant to control commerce and improvements upriver, was supposed to be permanent but was not formally organised until after 1918.
entries_new.anchor: Sulina mouth of the Danube, Romania (approximate)

entries_new.name: Saudi Arabian-Kuwaiti neutral zone
entries_new.founder: Uqair Convention of 1922, arranged by Britain
entries_new.recognition: Saudi Arabia and Kuwait by treaty
entries_new.mechanism: Two states left a stretch of border undefined and shared sovereignty over it.
entries_new.story: The Saudi Arabian-Kuwaiti neutral zone, also called the Divided Zone, covered 5,770 square kilometres between the Saudi and Kuwaiti borders and was left undefined by the Uqair Convention of 2 December 1922. Historian Daniel Yergin says it was drawn to accommodate Bedouin who moved between the two countries, with the two sharing sovereignty. Interest grew after oil was found at Burgan in Kuwait in 1938. Kuwait gave a concession in 1948 and Saudi Arabia in 1949, and the zone's first oil was shipped in January 1954.
entries_new.anchor: Saudi Arabia-Kuwait border

entries_new.name: Province of Pennsylvania (Penn proprietary)
entries_new.founder: William Penn
entries_new.stopped_by: American Revolution, 1776
entries_new.cost: Two beaver skins a year and one fifth of gold and silver ore
entries_new.mechanism: A royal charter granted land and wide powers of government to one proprietor in return for a small rent.
entries_new.story: The Province of Pennsylvania was founded for William Penn, who received the land through a 1681 grant from Charles II of England. The charter gave him wide freedom over administration, with the Crown to review the colony's laws every five years. He was to pay two beaver skins a year and one fifth of any gold and silver ore found. Penn intended a Holy Experiment under the guidance of the Quakers. By the American Revolution in 1776 the colony's borders ran across the Appalachian Mountains.
entries_new.anchor: Pennsylvania (source centre point)

entries_new.name: Province of New York (Duke of York's proprietary)
entries_new.founder: James, Duke of York
entries_new.stopped_by: Treaty of Paris, 1783
entries_new.challenge: Dutch West India Company, whose colony was taken in 1664
entries_new.recognition: Charles II of England; Treaty of Breda (1667)
entries_new.mechanism: A king gave his brother a colony taken by force from the Dutch, with the brother as its proprietor.
entries_new.story: The Province of New York was a British proprietary colony and later a royal colony. In 1664 Charles II of England and his brother James, Duke of York raised a fleet that took the Dutch colony of New Netherland, and Peter Stuyvesant surrendered without recognition from the Dutch West India Company. The province was renamed for the Duke as its proprietor. England's rule was established in fact in 1664 and in law in 1667 by the Treaty of Breda, and English common law applied from 1674. British claims ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
entries_new.anchor: New York (approximate)

entries_new.name: East and West Jersey proprietary provinces
entries_new.founder: Proprietors under the Quintipartite Deed; Robert Barclay was governor of East Jersey through most of the 1680s
entries_new.stopped_by: Proprietors surrendered to Queen Anne's government in 1702
entries_new.pop: About 3,500 in East Jersey in 1684 (not counting enslaved Africans)
entries_new.challenge: Residents, over land ownership and quitrents
entries_new.mechanism: Groups of proprietors held the right to rule and to sell land, with the Crown's authority behind them.
entries_new.story: East Jersey and West Jersey were two parts of the Province of New Jersey from 1674 to 1702, set up under the Quintipartite Deed. Where the border between them ran was often disputed. In East Jersey, the capital was Perth Amboy, and Robert Barclay and other Scottish proprietors began developing it in 1682. A 1684 survey estimated 3,500 people in about 700 families, not counting enslaved Africans. Residents and the mostly absent proprietors argued over land ownership and quitrents, which are yearly payments owed to the proprietors. The provinces were merged in 1702, when the proprietors surrendered to Queen Anne's government.
entries_new.anchor: East Jersey (source centre point; capital Perth Amboy)

entries_new.name: Province of New Hampshire (Mason proprietary)
entries_new.founder: John Mason (named it in 1629); Robert Tufton Mason (proprietor under the 1679 plan)
entries_new.stopped_by: Settlers' legal campaign against the proprietary structure
entries_new.mechanism: Charles II split the province from Massachusetts and gave it to a proprietor.
entries_new.story: John Mason named New Hampshire in 1629 as its first named proprietor. In 1679 Charles II partitioned Massachusetts to create the Province of New Hampshire, which was meant to be a proprietary colony owned by Robert Tufton Mason. The settlers, whose land claims had been granted under the authority of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, mounted a legal campaign and successfully resisted the proprietary structure. The province later became a royal colony and in 1776 an independent state.
entries_new.anchor: Province of New Hampshire (source centre point)

entries_new.name: Northern Neck Proprietary (Fairfax Grant)
entries_new.founder: Charles II of England, in exile; later Thomas Fairfax, 6th Lord Fairfax of Cameron
entries_new.stopped_by: Virginia Act of 1779 confiscated the unsettled land; the proprietary ended at Fairfax's death in 1781
entries_new.challenge: Boundary disputes; later the Virginia Act of 1779
entries_new.mechanism: A king granted a nobleman ownership of a huge tract with rights over its settlement.
entries_new.story: The Northern Neck Proprietary, also called the Fairfax Proprietary or Fairfax Grant, was a land grant first contrived in 1649 by the exiled Charles II. It covered all land between the Potomac and Rappahannock rivers in colonial Virginia, up to 5,000,000 acres, and a large area northwest of them. It became actual in 1660 when Charles was restored. By 1719 Thomas Fairfax, 6th Lord Fairfax of Cameron had inherited it. The boundaries were contested, and in 1746 the Fairfax Line fixed the western limit. Virginia confiscated the unsettled parts in 1779, and the proprietary ended with Fairfax's death in 1781.
entries_new.anchor: Northern Neck, Virginia (approximate)

entries_new.name: Port-Breton and the Marquis de Rays' New France
entries_new.founder: Marquis de Rays, French nobleman
entries_new.stopped_by: Colonists rescued by Australian authorities after 123 deaths
entries_new.pop: 340 Italian colonists on the ship India
entries_new.mechanism: A private colonisation scheme sold land and passage on promises about a settlement that did not exist.
entries_new.story: The Marquis de Rays, a French nobleman, tried to start a colony in the South Pacific that he called La Nouvelle France, on the island now called New Ireland in the Bismarck Archipelago. In 1880 the ship India sailed from Barcelona with 340 Italian colonists seeking relief from poor conditions in Italy. One hundred and twenty-three died before Australian authorities rescued the rest. The marquis is widely believed to have deliberately misled the colonists with literature describing a bustling settlement at Port Breton, with public buildings and wide roads. Port Breton was in fact at the remote south-western corner of New Ireland, where jungle mountains drop steeply into the sea.
entries_new.anchor: South-western New Ireland, Papua New Guinea (approximate)

entries_new.name: Glorioso Islands under Hippolyte Caltaux
entries_new.founder: Hippolyte Caltaux
entries_new.stopped_by: French claim of 1892 and regular French possession from 1960
entries_new.challenge: Comoros and Madagascar claim the islands today
entries_new.mechanism: A private settler held the islands as proprietor before France claimed them.
entries_new.story: The Glorioso Islands, also called the Glorieuses, are a group of islands and rocks of 5 square kilometres in the Indian Ocean. The Frenchman Hippolyte Caltaux settled and named them on 2 March 1880 and was their proprietor until 1891. France claimed them on 23 August 1892 as part of its colony of Madagascar. Caltaux was proprietor again from 1901 until his death. On 26 June 1960 the islands became a regular French possession. France controls them today, while Comoros and Madagascar also claim them.
entries_new.anchor: Glorioso Islands

entries_new.name: Pierre Du Gua de Monts's Acadia grant
entries_new.founder: Pierre Du Gua de Monts
entries_new.stopped_by: Monopoly revoked in 1607
entries_new.mechanism: A king granted one man a colonisation monopoly and a title over a large stretch of North America.
entries_new.story: In 1603 Henry IV of France granted Pierre Du Gua de Monts the exclusive right to colonise lands in North America between 40 and 60 degrees north. The king also gave him a monopoly in the fur trade there and named him Lieutenant General for Acadia and New France. In return de Monts promised to bring 60 new colonists a year. The monopoly was revoked in 1607 and the colony failed, but in 1608 he sponsored Samuel de Champlain to open a colony at Quebec.

entries_new.name: Province of Carolina (Lords Proprietors)
entries_new.founder: The Lords Proprietors of the Province of Carolina
entries_new.stopped_by: Partitioned into North and South Carolina in 1712
entries_new.mechanism: The Crown chartered proprietors to rule the province.
entries_new.story: Carolina was a province of Great Britain in America from 1663 until 1712. It was held by the Lords Proprietors of the Province of Carolina, who in 1712 partitioned it into the provinces of North Carolina and South Carolina. In the Proprietary colony article, Carolina is listed with Maryland as one of several colonies established under the proprietary system, in which individuals or companies received charters from the Crown with authority to choose governors and officials. Its territory now makes up a large part of seven US states.
